analysis.one_liner: Lets the President temporarily freeze gasoline and petroleum prices at pre-Hurricane Katrina levels.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2005 after Hurricane Katrina sent gas prices soaring, but was never taken up: it went to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and died there with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: After Hurricane Katrina shut refineries and pipelines, gasoline prices jumped sharply nationwide. This bill would have let the President order wholesale and retail gasoline and petroleum prices rolled back to, and frozen at, their August 27, 2005 levels until domestic petroleum supply recovered. Violators could be fined up to triple their illegal gains. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, drivers, households, and businesses that were paying sharply higher gas prices in the weeks after Katrina, plus anyone buying petroleum-based products whose costs rose with fuel prices. The freeze would also have let the government sue or fine sellers who charged above the frozen price, with penalties up to three times the gain.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have frozen wholesale and retail prices of gasoline and other petroleum products at or below their August 27, 2005 levels, before Katrina knocked out refineries and pipelines.

The bill's findings state that Katrina-caused shutdowns produced 'massive price increases' that caused 'severe hardships for millions of Americans' who need gasoline for transportation and daily necessities.
Sellers who willfully violated a freeze order could be fined up to three times the amount of their gain, and the government could seek court injunctions to stop violations.
The freeze was temporary by design: the President's authority would end once domestic petroleum supply returned to its pre-storm level.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners, wholesalers, and gasoline retailers, who would have had to sell at pre-storm prices during a period when supply was disrupted and market prices were much higher, giving up the windfall profits the disruption produced.

drawbacks.text: Price freezes can backfire during a genuine shortage: holding prices below market levels removes the signal that encourages conservation and discourages re-supply, which historically has risked lines and empty pumps.

The bill gives the President broad, largely unchecked power to set prices nationwide, and the endpoint is the President's own finding that supply has recovered rather than a fixed deadline or a congressional check.
By capping prices at pre-storm levels, the freeze would have shifted costs from consumers to the refining and retail sector at exactly the moment the industry faced storm damage and lost production.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the weeks after Katrina, a freeze would have directly relieved households from price spikes driven partly by genuine supply loss and partly by market concentration and opportunistic pricing. But the tool was blunt: it capped prices across the board during a real shortage, which economists warn can cause shortages and lines, and it handed the President open-ended pricing power with a self-declared end point. A narrower windfall-profits or anti-gouging approach was the more commonly argued alternative.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its energy subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maurice Hinchey introduced the bill on September 8, 2005, eleven days after the bill's pre-storm price date and about a week after Katrina struck the Gulf Coast refining region.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day; no other action was taken at the committee level.
On September 19, 2005 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it stayed for the rest of the 109th Congress.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil refiners, wholesalers, and gasoline retailers, who kept selling at the much higher post-Katrina prices the bill sought to roll back; the bill never advanced far enough to threaten those profits. Consumers continued paying the spike-era prices it would have capped.

for.name: Rep. Maurice D. Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it was referred to committee and died there.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of first referral, chaired by Rep. Joe Barton (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote, sending it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality where it stayed until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote of any kind, and it had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan lineup ever formed on the record.

industries.note: The freeze would have capped what refiners, wholesalers, and gas stations could charge at pre-storm levels during the post-Katrina price spike, forfeiting the windfall from Katrina's supply disruption. Because the bill never advanced, the industry kept the higher prices instead.

industries.industry: Consumers of gasoline and petroleum products
industries.note: Drivers, freight carriers, and fuel-dependent businesses paid the spike-era prices for the remainder of the emergency rather than the frozen pre-storm levels the bill would have restored.
